data.claim: A word-matched check on Bash tool_input.command, answered as permissionDecision deny with exit 0, refuses the commands without false positives on grep/commit-message mentions
data.falsifier: pkill reaches the shell, or 'git log --grep pkill' is refused
data.mechanism: Claude Code runs PreToolUse hooks before the tool and honours hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision=deny
data.probe_output: 28 passed (refused: 13 shapes incl. sudo, git -C, sh -c, xargs; allowed: 11 incl. grep/commit-msg/heredoc/review --force --reason)
data.question: Can a PreToolUse Bash hook refuse pkill/git stash/git push before they run?

evidence.note: ddflow brief --for-agent fleet-dx-a DX-forbidden-commands-hook returned the lessons (heartbeat, glob overlap); no rule conflicts
services/forbidden.py, [hooks] config section, pre_tool handler, pre-tool HookSpec, report overrides; tests/test_forbidden_commands.py 28 pass

chunk_findings.detail: `FB.record(...)` is called as soon as `FB.check` returns a refusal, before the dispatcher knows whether the harness can actually enforce it. In the dispatcher, when `HI.emit_deny(plan, event, res.deny)` returns `None` (the explicitly anticipated "no deny reply" case for a non-Claude harness), `res` is rewritten to `result="not enforceable"` and `out` stays the ordinary allow output — i.e. the command proceeds — but the refusal event has already been written to the log. Concretely: on a harness without a deny reply, an agent runs `pkill`, `FB.check` refuses, `FB.record` logs a refusal, `emit_deny` yields `None`, and the `pkill` still executes. `ddflow report` will then list a refusal for a command that was never refused, contradicting the stated goal that "each refusal is an event so ddflow report can list it" and making the audit trail assert enforcement that did not occur. A refusal record should be written only after `emit_deny` succeeds (or should carry the "not enforceable" outcome so the report can distinguish the two).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py:1008 (`_on_pre_tool` / dispatcher deny path)

chunk_findings.detail: The default deny-list is written so that only one entry is worktree-aware (`git reset --hard @primary`); every other entry — `pkill`, `killall`, `git stash`, `git push`, `--force`, `--force-with-lease` — is unscoped, so the PreToolUse guard refuses those commands *inside an item's worktree* as well. That collides with the recorded ACP decision [D-acp-r2], which states that the policy is "auto-allow inside the worktree and lease-covered repo files" and that state-changing commands go through the same authorization as the CLI. Concretely: an agent that has just started an item, is inside its own worktree, and runs the ordinary `git stash` before a rebase (or a `--force`-flagged command in that disposable tree) is now hard-denied by the hook, even though that location was designated the auto-allow zone — the guard is a stricter, harness-level authorization axis that the decision record does not account for. Either the guard should honor the worktree boundary the same way `@primary` does for the reset entry (or carry an explicit worktree exemption documented in the section), or the recorded decision needs amending to say the deny-list overrides worktree auto-allow.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/hooks.py:17 (`HooksConfig.forbidden_commands`)

chunk_findings.detail: The wrapper-option branch skips only the option word, not its value, despite the comment claiming "its value is dropped below": `elif w.startswith("-") and i and words[i - 1] in _WRAPPERS: i += 1`. Because the loop then hits the option's *value*, which matches none of the branch conditions, it `break`s, leaving the value as the command's own word. Given `sudo -u deploy pkill -f server`, `_head` returns `['deploy','pkill','-f','server']`, so `cmd = 'deploy' != 'pkill'` and `matches("pkill", ...)` is False — the refusal never fires and the agent's `pkill` runs. The same bypass works for every value-taking wrapper option: `nice -n 5 pkill`, `env -u PATH pkill`, `xargs -n 1 pkill`, and it also defeats the nested-shell detection in `_commands`, since `sudo -u x bash -c "pkill foo"` yields `body[0] == 'x'`, which is not in `_SHELLS`. This is exactly the class of destructive command the hook exists to stop, reachable with a one-word preamble. Fix: advance `i` past the option's value (`i += 2`, except for the value-less options), or drop the value in a following step.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_head

chunk_findings.detail:
`_strip_heredocs` treats *any* occurrence of `<<` as the start of a heredoc, computes a bogus terminator, and then discards every subsequent line until a line equals that bogus token — which never happens. Here-strings (`<<<`), arithmetic shifts (`$((1<<2))`), and `<<` inside a quoted argument all trigger it. Concretely, for the multi-line command

```
git commit -m "handle a<<b"
pkill foo
```

the first line yields `ends == ['b']`, so the second line fails `line.strip() == ends[0]` and is `continue`d — `pkill foo` is never handed to `_commands`, so `check` returns None and the command is allowed. `grep x <<< "$y"` followed by a forbidden command behaves identically. Since the whole point is that commands "after the fact" are refused, silently dropping the tail of a multi-line Bash invocation is a false negative in the enforcement path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_strip_heredocs

chunk_findings.detail: The per-session override cannot lift `@primary` entries as they are written in config. `check` normalizes the config entry with `entry = " ".join(raw.removesuffix(PRIMARY).split())`, so the default `git reset --hard @primary` becomes `git reset --hard`; but `_lifted` normalizes the env items verbatim, so `DDFLOW_HOOKS_ALLOW="git reset --hard @primary"` produces `lifted == {"git reset --hard @primary"}` and the test `if entry in lifted` is False. An operator who copies the configured entry (including the marker) to lift it for their session silently gets no override; only the non-obvious marker-less spelling works.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:check

chunk_findings.detail: The module makes `import ddflow` work in-process by inserting the repo root into `sys.path` (line 21), i.e. it explicitly supports running the suite from a checkout where `ddflow` is not installed. But the four hook tests shell out with `subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "ddflow", ...], cwd=repo, env={**os.environ, "DDFLOW_HOOKS_ALLOW": ""})`. `sys.path` is not inherited by a child process, and the only environment passed is `os.environ` plus `DDFLOW_HOOKS_ALLOW`; the repo root added at line 21 is never propagated (no `PYTHONPATH`). Because `python -m` puts the *current* directory on `sys.path`, and `cwd` is the freshly created temp repo (which contains no `ddflow` package, only `.ddflow`), the child raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'ddflow'`, exits 1, and `assert p.returncode == 0, p.stderr` fails. The same is true for `_repo()`'s `subprocess.run([... "init"], cwd=tmp_path, capture_output=True)` — and there the failure is silently swallowed (no `check=True`), so if it ever fails the following hook assertions fail with a misleading error instead of reporting the real cause. This affects exactly the environment the file's own `sys.path.insert` was written for (a plain `PYTHONPATH`-less checkout, or a run relying on pytest's `pythonpath`/rootdir insertion, which only patches the in-process `sys.path`); the tests only pass if `ddflow` happens to be pip-installed into the interpreter running pytest. Fix: add `str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1])` to `PYTHONPATH` in the env passed by `_hook`, and pass `check=True` (or assert) in `_repo`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_forbidden_commands.py:110 (`_hook`, and `_repo` at line 122)

chunk_findings.detail:
The knob's own doc defines the matching contract: each entry is a word sequence matched, in order, anywhere in the command, and an entry in `allowed_commands` wins over `forbidden_commands` ("A command matching an entry here is allowed even when it also matches a forbidden one"). Matching is done on the command text, with no comment stripping. So the default allow entry is a skeleton key over any single command (no `;`/`&&`/`|` splitting involved). Given the input

    pkill -f worker # ddflow review --force --reason

the words are `[pkill, -f, worker, #, ddflow, review, --force, --reason]`; the forbidden `pkill` matches, but the allowed sequence `ddflow review --force --reason` also matches, and allowed wins, so the command is permitted and `pkill` runs. The same trick whitelists `git push origin main # ddflow review --force --reason` and `rm -rf .ddflow # ddflow review --force --reason`. This is exactly the class of command the hook exists to stop (the stated evidence is subagents running `pkill`), and appending a comment — or any trailing tokens containing those four words in order — disables it. The exemption needs to be anchored to the whole command (or the allow list needs a distinct form), not to a subsequence found anywhere in it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/hooks.py (`allowed_commands` default, `"ddflow review --force --reason"`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The allow entry is order-fixed (`ddflow`, `review`, `--force`, `--reason`), while the forbidden entry `--force` matches "that flag anywhere". The documented safe command is valid ddflow in any flag order (argparse accepts it), but

    ddflow review --reason "extra round" --force

has words `[ddflow, review, --reason, extra, round, --force]`; the allowed sequence's required order (`--force` before `--reason`) is violated, so the allow entry does not match, the forbidden `--force` does, and the one command the config is explicitly meant to exempt is refused. A user who types the flags in the other (equally valid) order is pushed toward disabling the guard.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/hooks.py (`allowed_commands` default, order-sensitivity)

chunk_findings.detail: A wrapper's own option is skipped, but its *value* is not, so the value becomes the command's own word and the match fails. Input: `sudo -u root pkill foo` → words `["sudo","-u","root","pkill","foo"]`; `i=0` consumes `sudo`, the `elif` consumes `-u`, then `"root"` is neither a wrapper nor an assignment nor a flag, so the loop breaks and `head = ["root","pkill","foo"]`. `matches("pkill", …)` computes `cmd = "root" != "pkill"` and returns False, so the refusal is skipped. The same happens for `nice -n 5 pkill foo`, `env -u HOME pkill foo`, and `xargs -n 1 pkill foo` (the last also defeats the documented `xargs` wrapper handling). The inline comment at line 133 says the value "is dropped below", but nothing anywhere drops it — `_args` only strips git's global options.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:132 (`_head`, the `elif` branch)

chunk_findings.detail:
Any `<<` on a line is treated as a heredoc opener, even when it is not one (`<<<` here-strings, shift operators, `<<` inside quotes), and every following line is then silently discarded before `_commands` ever sees it. Input: a two-line script

    python -c "print(1<<3)"
    pkill -f myserver

For line 1, `line.split("<<")[1:]` gives `['3)"']`, so `ends = ['3)']`; line 2 does not equal `3)`, so it is `continue`d away, `_commands` returns only `[["python","-c","print(1<<3)"]]`, and `check` returns `None` although the second line is exactly the `pkill` the hook exists to refuse. The same happens with `bc <<< "2^10"` or a comment containing `<<` followed by a forbidden command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:86-90 (`_strip_heredocs`)

chunk_findings.detail: The `@primary` decision is made from the hook's own cwd only; nothing in the command line is consulted about where git will actually run. `matches` deliberately understands `-C` to find git's subcommand (line 165-171), but the directory it names is ignored here. Input, run with the hook's cwd inside an item worktree: `git -C /repo/primary reset --hard` — `matches` hits the `git reset --hard` entry, `only_primary` is true, `is_primary(worktree)` is False, so the command is allowed even though it resets the primary checkout. The same evasion works with `cd /repo/primary && git reset --hard`, because `cd` is merely another pipeline element and the `git` element is still evaluated against the unchanged cwd.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:236 (`is_primary(cwd or Path.cwd())`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The value returned by `HI.emit_deny(plan, "pre_tool", "")` is used only to gate the `FB.record(...)` call; the following context lines show the handler still unconditionally runs `msg = refusal.message()` and `return _HookResult(result="denied", deny=msg, note=msg)`. That decouples the audit trail from the enforcement, in a way that is wrong under either meaning of the guard:

- If `emit_deny` returns `None` because the deny could not be emitted (e.g. no harness/session context to emit into, or an emission failure), the command is still refused for the agent — `result="denied"` — but no refusal event is written, so `ddflow report` silently omits exactly the refusals the change exists to surface ("each refusal is an event so ddflow report can list it"). Input that demonstrates it: a Bash call matching `pkill` from a session/harness where `emit_deny` cannot produce output → the hook still denies, `FB.record` is skipped, and the refusal is invisible to the report.
- If instead `None` is the "refusal does not hold" signal (the comment "only a refusal that holds is recorded" implies non-`None` == holds, hence `None` == does not hold — i.e. an operator/session override or an `allowed_commands` match), then the guard correctly suppresses the recording but the code then defeats the override by returning `result="denied"` anyway, so the per-session override the intent promises never takes effect.

In both cases the guard's result should drive the decision as well as the recording; as written, one of enforcement or override is silently broken.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py:959 (PreToolUse refusal handler, `_HookResult(result="denied", ...)`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `_VALUED` set is applied uniformly to every wrapper, but the short options in it do not take a value for all of them. `-n` is valued for `nice`/`xargs` (e.g. `nice -n 5`) but is a *flag* for `sudo` (`sudo -n` = non-interactive), and the same is true of `-s`, `-t`, `-p` for `sudo`/`xargs`. Since `_head` does `i += 2 if w in _VALUED else 1` whenever `wrapped` is true, it silently eats the real command as if it were the option's value.

Concretely, for the very command this hook exists to stop: `words = ["sudo", "-n", "pkill"]` → `i=0` (`sudo`, `wrapped=True`), `i=1` (`-n` in `_VALUED`, `i=3`), loop ends → `_head` returns `[]`, so the entry `pkill` never matches and the command is allowed. With an argument, `sudo -n pkill -f <pattern>` → `["sudo","-n","pkill","-f","x"]`: `-n` skips `pkill`, `-f` skips one, and `_head` returns `["x"]` — still no `pkill`. The old code (`w.startswith("-") and words[i-1] in _WRAPPERS → i += 1`, one word at a time) returned `["pkill"]` here, so this is a regression introduced by the change: a previously-refused command now passes the hook. The same misparse hits `time -p pkill` (`-p` is POSIX output format, takes no argument) and `xargs -t pkill`/`xargs -p pkill`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py — `_VALUED` / `_head`

chunk_findings.detail:
`_elsewhere` decides "may act on another checkout" by exact word membership, but git accepts the path attached with `=`: `--git-dir=<path>`, `--work-tree=<path>` (likewise attached `-C<path>`). Those tokens never compare equal to `"-C"`/`"--git-dir"`/`"--work-tree"`, so from inside an item's worktree the command

    git --git-dir=/repo/.git --work-tree=/repo reset --hard

is not classified as "elsewhere". The `@primary` entry (`git reset --hard`) is reached, `_elsewhere(cmds)` returns False, `is_primary(cwd)` is evaluated with cwd = the worktree → False, the `if not primary: continue` branch runs, and the hard reset of the primary checkout is allowed — exactly the case the new helper's own docstring claims to cover ("`git -C dir`"). If the matcher instead refuses to consume the leading `--git-dir=...` option, the argv doesn't match the entry at all, so the command is still not refused; the outcome is the same either way. Only the space-separated spelling (`git --git-dir /repo/.git --work-tree /repo reset --hard`) can ever reach the tuple comparison, so the `--git-dir`/`--work-tree` elements of the check are effectively unreachable for the syntax git actually documents.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py::_elsewhere

chunk_findings.detail: The change replaces a whole-list equality check (`data["hooks"]["PreToolUse"] == EXISTING["hooks"]["PreToolUse"]`) with an index-0-only comparison, so the test no longer detects that pre-existing `PreToolUse` hooks beyond the first survive the install. Concretely: give the fixture a settings file whose `PreToolUse` already holds two hooks (e.g. the user's formatter hook followed by a linter hook); if the installer rewrites the array as `[theirs[0], ours]` — silently dropping the linter entry — the new assertion still passes (`[0]` matches, `len(_ours(data)) == 1`), while the equivalent guarantee for `SessionStart` is still checked in full on the very next lines (`assert theirs == EXISTING["hooks"]["SessionStart"][0]["hooks"], "their hooks were edited"`). The comment claims "theirs stays first and untouched", but nothing in the assertion verifies "untouched" for anything past index 0, which is precisely the requirement this PreToolUse guard installs beside (operator-supplied hooks must not be clobbered). A length/chained-equality check against the original list (or comparing the preserved prefix) would restore the coverage.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_claude_hooks.py:82 (assertion on `data["hooks"]["PreToolUse"][0]`)

chunk_findings.detail: The default pair refuses every `--force` but exempts exactly one command, `ddflow review --force --reason`. The added doc asserts this is "the one `--force` ddflow itself documents", but the same `--explain` listing 1300 lines above it contradicts that: `lease.resume_own` says "Off: the holder needs --force too, as before", i.e. with `resume_own = false` (a supported project setting) the documented way for a holder to resume its own lapsed lease is `ddflow claim <id> --force`, and `lease.resume_own` / `recover` are the crash-recovery paths this workflow exists for. Concretely: a project with `lease.resume_own = false`, an agent whose lease lapsed during a long gate runs `ddflow claim T1 --force`; the PreToolUse hook matches the `--force` entry, `allowed_commands` does not exempt `ddflow claim`, and the call is refused with no safe alternative named — recovery is blocked until the operator sets `DDFLOW_HOOKS_ALLOW` for the session, i.e. precisely in the incident where the queue is stalled. Either `ddflow claim --force` (and any other ddflow-internal `--force` the docs tell agents to run) belongs in `allowed_commands`, or the `--force` entry needs to be scoped to git/unknown commands rather than "that flag anywhere".

chunk_findings.detail:
The allow entry is order-fixed (`ddflow`, `review`, `--force`, `--reason`), while the forbidden entry `--force` matches "that flag anywhere". The documented safe command is valid ddflow in any flag order (argparse accepts it), but

    ddflow review --reason "extra round" --force

has words `[ddflow, review, --reason, extra, round, --force]`; the allowed sequence's required order (`--force` before `--reason`) is violated, so the allow entry does not match, the forbidden `--force` does, and the one command the config is explicitly meant to exempt is refused. A user who types the flags in the other (equally valid) order is pushed toward disabling the guard.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/hooks.py (`allowed_commands` default, order-sensitivity)

chunk_findings.detail: A wrapper's own option is skipped, but its *value* is not, so the value becomes the command's own word and the match fails. Input: `sudo -u root pkill foo` → words `["sudo","-u","root","pkill","foo"]`; `i=0` consumes `sudo`, the `elif` consumes `-u`, then `"root"` is neither a wrapper nor an assignment nor a flag, so the loop breaks and `head = ["root","pkill","foo"]`. `matches("pkill", …)` computes `cmd = "root" != "pkill"` and returns False, so the refusal is skipped. The same happens for `nice -n 5 pkill foo`, `env -u HOME pkill foo`, and `xargs -n 1 pkill foo` (the last also defeats the documented `xargs` wrapper handling). The inline comment at line 133 says the value "is dropped below", but nothing anywhere drops it — `_args` only strips git's global options.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:132 (`_head`, the `elif` branch)

chunk_findings.detail:
Any `<<` on a line is treated as a heredoc opener, even when it is not one (`<<<` here-strings, shift operators, `<<` inside quotes), and every following line is then silently discarded before `_commands` ever sees it. Input: a two-line script

    python -c "print(1<<3)"
    pkill -f myserver

For line 1, `line.split("<<")[1:]` gives `['3)"']`, so `ends = ['3)']`; line 2 does not equal `3)`, so it is `continue`d away, `_commands` returns only `[["python","-c","print(1<<3)"]]`, and `check` returns `None` although the second line is exactly the `pkill` the hook exists to refuse. The same happens with `bc <<< "2^10"` or a comment containing `<<` followed by a forbidden command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:86-90 (`_strip_heredocs`)

chunk_findings.detail: The `@primary` decision is made from the hook's own cwd only; nothing in the command line is consulted about where git will actually run. `matches` deliberately understands `-C` to find git's subcommand (line 165-171), but the directory it names is ignored here. Input, run with the hook's cwd inside an item worktree: `git -C /repo/primary reset --hard` — `matches` hits the `git reset --hard` entry, `only_primary` is true, `is_primary(worktree)` is False, so the command is allowed even though it resets the primary checkout. The same evasion works with `cd /repo/primary && git reset --hard`, because `cd` is merely another pipeline element and the `git` element is still evaluated against the unchanged cwd.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:236 (`is_primary(cwd or Path.cwd())`)

chunk_findings.detail: The deny path has been restructured so that `HI.emit_deny(plan, "pre_tool", "")` is evaluated *outside* the `try/except` that the rest of the refusal bookkeeping deliberately keeps inside ("an unrecorded refusal is still a refusal"), and its return value now gates `FB.record`. Two concrete problems follow. (1) If `emit_deny` raises — it is the piece that consults the hook plan/descriptors and emits output, i.e. exactly the I/O-bearing call — the exception escapes before the line `return _HookResult(result="denied", deny=msg, note=msg)` ever runs. Harnesses model a PreToolUse hook that exits with a generic error (not the deny exit) as a *non-blocking* error, so the forbidden command proceeds: `pkill` (or any configured forbidden command) is allowed through precisely when the emission step fails. The original code wrapped the log/record work in `except Exception: pass` for exactly this reason; the new call removes that protection from the critical path. (2) On the branch where `emit_deny` returns `None`, the function still returns `_HookResult(result="denied", ...)`, so from the caller's perspective the refusal held, yet `FB.record` is skipped and no event exists. Given the stated purpose ("each refusal is an event so ddflow report can list it"), a refusal in that branch is invisible to `ddflow report`, which is the evidence the change was motivated by (three subagents running `pkill`). Either the guard should not gate recording, or the `denied` result should not be returned when `emit_deny` yields `None` — as written the two disagree.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py:959

chunk_findings.detail: `_VALUED` is the union of every wrapper's option-that-takes-a-value, and `_head` applies it to whichever wrapper it just saw, no matter which one it was. So a wrapper flag that takes *no* value now swallows the next word, which is the command being checked. Concretely `sudo -n bash -c 'pkill -f worker'`: `i` stops on `-n` (member of `_VALUED`), jumps `i += 2`, dropping `bash`, and `_head` returns `['pkill -f worker']`; `body[0]` is therefore not in `_SHELLS`, the `-c` string is never re-parsed, and no `pkill` command is ever produced for the matcher. The old `_head` returned `['bash', '-c', 'pkill -f worker']` here and the command was refused. The plain forms regress too: `sudo -n pkill -f worker` → head `['worker']`, `time -p pkill worker` → head `['worker']` (`-p` is `time`'s POSIX flag), `command -p pkill -f worker` (`-p` is `command`'s default-PATH flag), `xargs -t pkill` (`-t` prints, takes no value). None of those were missed before this diff.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_head / _VALUED

chunk_findings.detail: `_MAX_DEPTH` was deleted and nesting is now a boolean, so only one `sh -c` / `bash -c` level is looked into (the removal is even documented: "a deeper one is not looked into"). Previously depth 0–2 were expanded. Input `bash -c "bash -c 'pkill -f worker'"`: the outer level yields `['bash','-c',"bash -c 'pkill -f worker'"]`, the recursive call runs with `nested=True`, and the inner `bash -c 'pkill …'` is never expanded, so no `pkill` command is produced and the hook stays silent, where the previous three-level expansion produced `['pkill','-f','worker']` and refused it. One extra shell layer is a trivial bypass of a hook whose stated purpose is enforcement.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_commands

chunk_findings.detail: The capture group `([A-Za-z_]\w*)` stops at the first non-word character, so a delimiter that `shlex`-style quoting allows but the regex cannot express is truncated. For `cat <<EOF-2` the group is `EOF`; the "only a terminator line that really follows makes it a heredoc" test then searches for a line equal to `EOF`, finds none (the real terminator is `EOF-2`), and drops nothing. The body is handed to `_commands` as commands, so a document heredoc such as `cat <<EOF-2` / `pkill -f worker` / `EOF-2` makes the hook refuse a line bash would never execute as a command. The pre-change parser (`p.lstrip("-").strip().split(" ")[0].strip("'\"")`) recovered the full `EOF-2` and stripped the body correctly; the same misparse applies to `<<'END.JSON'` and similar.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_HEREDOC

chunk_findings.detail: `_elsewhere()` declares the command may act on another checkout whenever *any* word of *any* segment in the line is exactly `-C`, `--git-dir` or `--work-tree`, and the caller then does `primary = _elsewhere(cmds) or is_primary(...)`. `-C` is a flag of many unrelated tools. Input: in an item worktree the agent runs `make -C build && git reset --hard` (or `tar -C /tmp -xf x.tar && git reset --hard`, or `grep -C 3 foo && git reset --hard`). `cmds` is `[["make","-C","build"],["git","reset","--hard"]]`, so `_elsewhere` returns True even though nothing outside the worktree is touched, the `git reset --hard @primary` entry is judged applicable and the hook refuses a command that `is_primary(cwd)` correctly reported as non-primary and allowed before this change. The docstring's premise ("the cwd cannot say which one") does not hold when `-C` belongs to another program, and because `_elsewhere` is fed the whole `cmds` list, a `cd`/`-C` in one pipeline segment also taints an unrelated `git reset --hard` segment.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_elsewhere (the `-C` token scan)

chunk_findings.detail: The check is exact token equality, so the idiomatic attached forms `--git-dir=<path>` and `--work-tree=<path>` are never recognised, and the cwd of a worktree then decides the answer. Input: from an item worktree, `git --git-dir=/main/.git --work-tree=/main reset --hard` — the entry `git reset --hard @primary` is the exact thing this rule exists to refuse, but the tokens are `--git-dir=/main/.git` / `--work-tree=/main` (not `--git-dir` / `--work-tree`), so `_elsewhere` returns False, `is_primary(cwd)` returns False, and the command that resets the primary is allowed. The same class covers `GIT_DIR=/main/.git GIT_WORK_TREE=/main git reset --hard`, which contains no matching token at all. Since the new `-C` clause only makes sense if `matches()` skips leading option tokens (otherwise `git -C dir reset --hard` would never match the entry either), these attached-option commands do reach the `only_primary` branch and are wrongly let through.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_elsewhere (attached option forms)

chunk_findings.detail: `FB.record(...)` is called as soon as `FB.check` returns a refusal, before the dispatcher knows whether the harness can actually enforce it. In the dispatcher, when `HI.emit_deny(plan, event, res.deny)` returns `None` (the explicitly anticipated "no deny reply" case for a non-Claude harness), `res` is rewritten to `result="not enforceable"` and `out` stays the ordinary allow output — i.e. the command proceeds — but the refusal event has already been written to the log. Concretely: on a harness without a deny reply, an agent runs `pkill`, `FB.check` refuses, `FB.record` logs a refusal, `emit_deny` yields `None`, and the `pkill` still executes. `ddflow report` will then list a refusal for a command that was never refused, contradicting the stated goal that "each refusal is an event so ddflow report can list it" and making the audit trail assert enforcement that did not occur. A refusal record should be written only after `emit_deny` succeeds (or should carry the "not enforceable" outcome so the report can distinguish the two).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py:1008 (`_on_pre_tool` / dispatcher deny path)

chunk_findings.detail: The default deny-list is written so that only one entry is worktree-aware (`git reset --hard @primary`); every other entry — `pkill`, `killall`, `git stash`, `git push`, `--force`, `--force-with-lease` — is unscoped, so the PreToolUse guard refuses those commands *inside an item's worktree* as well. That collides with the recorded ACP decision [D-acp-r2], which states that the policy is "auto-allow inside the worktree and lease-covered repo files" and that state-changing commands go through the same authorization as the CLI. Concretely: an agent that has just started an item, is inside its own worktree, and runs the ordinary `git stash` before a rebase (or a `--force`-flagged command in that disposable tree) is now hard-denied by the hook, even though that location was designated the auto-allow zone — the guard is a stricter, harness-level authorization axis that the decision record does not account for. Either the guard should honor the worktree boundary the same way `@primary` does for the reset entry (or carry an explicit worktree exemption documented in the section), or the recorded decision needs amending to say the deny-list overrides worktree auto-allow.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/hooks.py:17 (`HooksConfig.forbidden_commands`)

chunk_findings.detail: The wrapper-option branch skips only the option word, not its value, despite the comment claiming "its value is dropped below": `elif w.startswith("-") and i and words[i - 1] in _WRAPPERS: i += 1`. Because the loop then hits the option's *value*, which matches none of the branch conditions, it `break`s, leaving the value as the command's own word. Given `sudo -u deploy pkill -f server`, `_head` returns `['deploy','pkill','-f','server']`, so `cmd = 'deploy' != 'pkill'` and `matches("pkill", ...)` is False — the refusal never fires and the agent's `pkill` runs. The same bypass works for every value-taking wrapper option: `nice -n 5 pkill`, `env -u PATH pkill`, `xargs -n 1 pkill`, and it also defeats the nested-shell detection in `_commands`, since `sudo -u x bash -c "pkill foo"` yields `body[0] == 'x'`, which is not in `_SHELLS`. This is exactly the class of destructive command the hook exists to stop, reachable with a one-word preamble. Fix: advance `i` past the option's value (`i += 2`, except for the value-less options), or drop the value in a following step.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_head

chunk_findings.detail:
`_strip_heredocs` treats *any* occurrence of `<<` as the start of a heredoc, computes a bogus terminator, and then discards every subsequent line until a line equals that bogus token — which never happens. Here-strings (`<<<`), arithmetic shifts (`$((1<<2))`), and `<<` inside a quoted argument all trigger it. Concretely, for the multi-line command

```
git commit -m "handle a<<b"
pkill foo
```

the first line yields `ends == ['b']`, so the second line fails `line.strip() == ends[0]` and is `continue`d — `pkill foo` is never handed to `_commands`, so `check` returns None and the command is allowed. `grep x <<< "$y"` followed by a forbidden command behaves identically. Since the whole point is that commands "after the fact" are refused, silently dropping the tail of a multi-line Bash invocation is a false negative in the enforcement path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_strip_heredocs

chunk_findings.detail: The per-session override cannot lift `@primary` entries as they are written in config. `check` normalizes the config entry with `entry = " ".join(raw.removesuffix(PRIMARY).split())`, so the default `git reset --hard @primary` becomes `git reset --hard`; but `_lifted` normalizes the env items verbatim, so `DDFLOW_HOOKS_ALLOW="git reset --hard @primary"` produces `lifted == {"git reset --hard @primary"}` and the test `if entry in lifted` is False. An operator who copies the configured entry (including the marker) to lift it for their session silently gets no override; only the non-obvious marker-less spelling works.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:check

chunk_findings.detail: The module makes `import ddflow` work in-process by inserting the repo root into `sys.path` (line 21), i.e. it explicitly supports running the suite from a checkout where `ddflow` is not installed. But the four hook tests shell out with `subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "ddflow", ...], cwd=repo, env={**os.environ, "DDFLOW_HOOKS_ALLOW": ""})`. `sys.path` is not inherited by a child process, and the only environment passed is `os.environ` plus `DDFLOW_HOOKS_ALLOW`; the repo root added at line 21 is never propagated (no `PYTHONPATH`). Because `python -m` puts the *current* directory on `sys.path`, and `cwd` is the freshly created temp repo (which contains no `ddflow` package, only `.ddflow`), the child raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'ddflow'`, exits 1, and `assert p.returncode == 0, p.stderr` fails. The same is true for `_repo()`'s `subprocess.run([... "init"], cwd=tmp_path, capture_output=True)` — and there the failure is silently swallowed (no `check=True`), so if it ever fails the following hook assertions fail with a misleading error instead of reporting the real cause. This affects exactly the environment the file's own `sys.path.insert` was written for (a plain `PYTHONPATH`-less checkout, or a run relying on pytest's `pythonpath`/rootdir insertion, which only patches the in-process `sys.path`); the tests only pass if `ddflow` happens to be pip-installed into the interpreter running pytest. Fix: add `str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1])` to `PYTHONPATH` in the env passed by `_hook`, and pass `check=True` (or assert) in `_repo`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_forbidden_commands.py:110 (`_hook`, and `_repo` at line 122)

chunk_findings.detail:
The value returned by `HI.emit_deny(plan, "pre_tool", "")` is used only to gate the `FB.record(...)` call; the following context lines show the handler still unconditionally runs `msg = refusal.message()` and `return _HookResult(result="denied", deny=msg, note=msg)`. That decouples the audit trail from the enforcement, in a way that is wrong under either meaning of the guard:

- If `emit_deny` returns `None` because the deny could not be emitted (e.g. no harness/session context to emit into, or an emission failure), the command is still refused for the agent — `result="denied"` — but no refusal event is written, so `ddflow report` silently omits exactly the refusals the change exists to surface ("each refusal is an event so ddflow report can list it"). Input that demonstrates it: a Bash call matching `pkill` from a session/harness where `emit_deny` cannot produce output → the hook still denies, `FB.record` is skipped, and the refusal is invisible to the report.
- If instead `None` is the "refusal does not hold" signal (the comment "only a refusal that holds is recorded" implies non-`None` == holds, hence `None` == does not hold — i.e. an operator/session override or an `allowed_commands` match), then the guard correctly suppresses the recording but the code then defeats the override by returning `result="denied"` anyway, so the per-session override the intent promises never takes effect.

In both cases the guard's result should drive the decision as well as the recording; as written, one of enforcement or override is silently broken.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py:959 (PreToolUse refusal handler, `_HookResult(result="denied", ...)`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `_VALUED` set is applied uniformly to every wrapper, but the short options in it do not take a value for all of them. `-n` is valued for `nice`/`xargs` (e.g. `nice -n 5`) but is a *flag* for `sudo` (`sudo -n` = non-interactive), and the same is true of `-s`, `-t`, `-p` for `sudo`/`xargs`. Since `_head` does `i += 2 if w in _VALUED else 1` whenever `wrapped` is true, it silently eats the real command as if it were the option's value.

Concretely, for the very command this hook exists to stop: `words = ["sudo", "-n", "pkill"]` → `i=0` (`sudo`, `wrapped=True`), `i=1` (`-n` in `_VALUED`, `i=3`), loop ends → `_head` returns `[]`, so the entry `pkill` never matches and the command is allowed. With an argument, `sudo -n pkill -f <pattern>` → `["sudo","-n","pkill","-f","x"]`: `-n` skips `pkill`, `-f` skips one, and `_head` returns `["x"]` — still no `pkill`. The old code (`w.startswith("-") and words[i-1] in _WRAPPERS → i += 1`, one word at a time) returned `["pkill"]` here, so this is a regression introduced by the change: a previously-refused command now passes the hook. The same misparse hits `time -p pkill` (`-p` is POSIX output format, takes no argument) and `xargs -t pkill`/`xargs -p pkill`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py — `_VALUED` / `_head`

chunk_findings.detail:
`_elsewhere` decides "may act on another checkout" by exact word membership, but git accepts the path attached with `=`: `--git-dir=<path>`, `--work-tree=<path>` (likewise attached `-C<path>`). Those tokens never compare equal to `"-C"`/`"--git-dir"`/`"--work-tree"`, so from inside an item's worktree the command

    git --git-dir=/repo/.git --work-tree=/repo reset --hard

is not classified as "elsewhere". The `@primary` entry (`git reset --hard`) is reached, `_elsewhere(cmds)` returns False, `is_primary(cwd)` is evaluated with cwd = the worktree → False, the `if not primary: continue` branch runs, and the hard reset of the primary checkout is allowed — exactly the case the new helper's own docstring claims to cover ("`git -C dir`"). If the matcher instead refuses to consume the leading `--git-dir=...` option, the argv doesn't match the entry at all, so the command is still not refused; the outcome is the same either way. Only the space-separated spelling (`git --git-dir /repo/.git --work-tree /repo reset --hard`) can ever reach the tuple comparison, so the `--git-dir`/`--work-tree` elements of the check are effectively unreachable for the syntax git actually documents.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py::_elsewhere

chunk_findings.detail: The change replaces a whole-list equality check (`data["hooks"]["PreToolUse"] == EXISTING["hooks"]["PreToolUse"]`) with an index-0-only comparison, so the test no longer detects that pre-existing `PreToolUse` hooks beyond the first survive the install. Concretely: give the fixture a settings file whose `PreToolUse` already holds two hooks (e.g. the user's formatter hook followed by a linter hook); if the installer rewrites the array as `[theirs[0], ours]` — silently dropping the linter entry — the new assertion still passes (`[0]` matches, `len(_ours(data)) == 1`), while the equivalent guarantee for `SessionStart` is still checked in full on the very next lines (`assert theirs == EXISTING["hooks"]["SessionStart"][0]["hooks"], "their hooks were edited"`). The comment claims "theirs stays first and untouched", but nothing in the assertion verifies "untouched" for anything past index 0, which is precisely the requirement this PreToolUse guard installs beside (operator-supplied hooks must not be clobbered). A length/chained-equality check against the original list (or comparing the preserved prefix) would restore the coverage.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_claude_hooks.py:82 (assertion on `data["hooks"]["PreToolUse"][0]`)

chunk_findings.detail: The default pair refuses every `--force` but exempts exactly one command, `ddflow review --force --reason`. The added doc asserts this is "the one `--force` ddflow itself documents", but the same `--explain` listing 1300 lines above it contradicts that: `lease.resume_own` says "Off: the holder needs --force too, as before", i.e. with `resume_own = false` (a supported project setting) the documented way for a holder to resume its own lapsed lease is `ddflow claim <id> --force`, and `lease.resume_own` / `recover` are the crash-recovery paths this workflow exists for. Concretely: a project with `lease.resume_own = false`, an agent whose lease lapsed during a long gate runs `ddflow claim T1 --force`; the PreToolUse hook matches the `--force` entry, `allowed_commands` does not exempt `ddflow claim`, and the call is refused with no safe alternative named — recovery is blocked until the operator sets `DDFLOW_HOOKS_ALLOW` for the session, i.e. precisely in the incident where the queue is stalled. Either `ddflow claim --force` (and any other ddflow-internal `--force` the docs tell agents to run) belongs in `allowed_commands`, or the `--force` entry needs to be scoped to git/unknown commands rather than "that flag anywhere".
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_uc_surf_setup_ops_transcript.json:1451 (`hooks.forbidden_commands` / `hooks.allowed_commands`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The knob's own doc defines the matching contract: each entry is a word sequence matched, in order, anywhere in the command, and an entry in `allowed_commands` wins over `forbidden_commands` ("A command matching an entry here is allowed even when it also matches a forbidden one"). Matching is done on the command text, with no comment stripping. So the default allow entry is a skeleton key over any single command (no `;`/`&&`/`|` splitting involved). Given the input

    pkill -f worker # ddflow review --force --reason

the words are `[pkill, -f, worker, #, ddflow, review, --force, --reason]`; the forbidden `pkill` matches, but the allowed sequence `ddflow review --force --reason` also matches, and allowed wins, so the command is permitted and `pkill` runs. The same trick whitelists `git push origin main # ddflow review --force --reason` and `rm -rf .ddflow # ddflow review --force --reason`. This is exactly the class of command the hook exists to stop (the stated evidence is subagents running `pkill`), and appending a comment — or any trailing tokens containing those four words in order — disables it. The exemption needs to be anchored to the whole command (or the allow list needs a distinct form), not to a subsequence found anywhere in it.

    python -c "print(1<<3)"

For line 1, `line.split("<<")[1:]` gives `['3)"']`, so `ends = ['3)']`; line 2 does not equal `3)`, so it is `continue`d away, `_commands` returns only `[["python","-c","print(1<<3)"]]`, and `check` returns `None` although the second line is exactly the `pkill` the hook exists to refuse. The same happens with `bc <<< "2^10"` or a comment containing `<<` followed by a forbidden command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:86-90 (`_strip_heredocs`)

chunk_findings.detail: The `@primary` decision is made from the hook's own cwd only; nothing in the command line is consulted about where git will actually run. `matches` deliberately understands `-C` to find git's subcommand (line 165-171), but the directory it names is ignored here. Input, run with the hook's cwd inside an item worktree: `git -C /repo/primary reset --hard` — `matches` hits the `git reset --hard` entry, `only_primary` is true, `is_primary(worktree)` is False, so the command is allowed even though it resets the primary checkout. The same evasion works with `cd /repo/primary && git reset --hard`, because `cd` is merely another pipeline element and the `git` element is still evaluated against the unchanged cwd.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:236 (`is_primary(cwd or Path.cwd())`)

chunk_findings.detail: The deny path has been restructured so that `HI.emit_deny(plan, "pre_tool", "")` is evaluated *outside* the `try/except` that the rest of the refusal bookkeeping deliberately keeps inside ("an unrecorded refusal is still a refusal"), and its return value now gates `FB.record`. Two concrete problems follow. (1) If `emit_deny` raises — it is the piece that consults the hook plan/descriptors and emits output, i.e. exactly the I/O-bearing call — the exception escapes before the line `return _HookResult(result="denied", deny=msg, note=msg)` ever runs. Harnesses model a PreToolUse hook that exits with a generic error (not the deny exit) as a *non-blocking* error, so the forbidden command proceeds: `pkill` (or any configured forbidden command) is allowed through precisely when the emission step fails. The original code wrapped the log/record work in `except Exception: pass` for exactly this reason; the new call removes that protection from the critical path. (2) On the branch where `emit_deny` returns `None`, the function still returns `_HookResult(result="denied", ...)`, so from the caller's perspective the refusal held, yet `FB.record` is skipped and no event exists. Given the stated purpose ("each refusal is an event so ddflow report can list it"), a refusal in that branch is invisible to `ddflow report`, which is the evidence the change was motivated by (three subagents running `pkill`). Either the guard should not gate recording, or the `denied` result should not be returned when `emit_deny` yields `None` — as written the two disagree.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py:959

chunk_findings.detail: `_VALUED` is the union of every wrapper's option-that-takes-a-value, and `_head` applies it to whichever wrapper it just saw, no matter which one it was. So a wrapper flag that takes *no* value now swallows the next word, which is the command being checked. Concretely `sudo -n bash -c 'pkill -f worker'`: `i` stops on `-n` (member of `_VALUED`), jumps `i += 2`, dropping `bash`, and `_head` returns `['pkill -f worker']`; `body[0]` is therefore not in `_SHELLS`, the `-c` string is never re-parsed, and no `pkill` command is ever produced for the matcher. The old `_head` returned `['bash', '-c', 'pkill -f worker']` here and the command was refused. The plain forms regress too: `sudo -n pkill -f worker` → head `['worker']`, `time -p pkill worker` → head `['worker']` (`-p` is `time`'s POSIX flag), `command -p pkill -f worker` (`-p` is `command`'s default-PATH flag), `xargs -t pkill` (`-t` prints, takes no value). None of those were missed before this diff.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_head / _VALUED

chunk_findings.detail: `_MAX_DEPTH` was deleted and nesting is now a boolean, so only one `sh -c` / `bash -c` level is looked into (the removal is even documented: "a deeper one is not looked into"). Previously depth 0–2 were expanded. Input `bash -c "bash -c 'pkill -f worker'"`: the outer level yields `['bash','-c',"bash -c 'pkill -f worker'"]`, the recursive call runs with `nested=True`, and the inner `bash -c 'pkill …'` is never expanded, so no `pkill` command is produced and the hook stays silent, where the previous three-level expansion produced `['pkill','-f','worker']` and refused it. One extra shell layer is a trivial bypass of a hook whose stated purpose is enforcement.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_commands

chunk_findings.detail: The capture group `([A-Za-z_]\w*)` stops at the first non-word character, so a delimiter that `shlex`-style quoting allows but the regex cannot express is truncated. For `cat <<EOF-2` the group is `EOF`; the "only a terminator line that really follows makes it a heredoc" test then searches for a line equal to `EOF`, finds none (the real terminator is `EOF-2`), and drops nothing. The body is handed to `_commands` as commands, so a document heredoc such as `cat <<EOF-2` / `pkill -f worker` / `EOF-2` makes the hook refuse a line bash would never execute as a command. The pre-change parser (`p.lstrip("-").strip().split(" ")[0].strip("'\"")`) recovered the full `EOF-2` and stripped the body correctly; the same misparse applies to `<<'END.JSON'` and similar.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_HEREDOC

chunk_findings.detail: `_elsewhere()` declares the command may act on another checkout whenever *any* word of *any* segment in the line is exactly `-C`, `--git-dir` or `--work-tree`, and the caller then does `primary = _elsewhere(cmds) or is_primary(...)`. `-C` is a flag of many unrelated tools. Input: in an item worktree the agent runs `make -C build && git reset --hard` (or `tar -C /tmp -xf x.tar && git reset --hard`, or `grep -C 3 foo && git reset --hard`). `cmds` is `[["make","-C","build"],["git","reset","--hard"]]`, so `_elsewhere` returns True even though nothing outside the worktree is touched, the `git reset --hard @primary` entry is judged applicable and the hook refuses a command that `is_primary(cwd)` correctly reported as non-primary and allowed before this change. The docstring's premise ("the cwd cannot say which one") does not hold when `-C` belongs to another program, and because `_elsewhere` is fed the whole `cmds` list, a `cd`/`-C` in one pipeline segment also taints an unrelated `git reset --hard` segment.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_elsewhere (the `-C` token scan)

chunk_findings.detail: The check is exact token equality, so the idiomatic attached forms `--git-dir=<path>` and `--work-tree=<path>` are never recognised, and the cwd of a worktree then decides the answer. Input: from an item worktree, `git --git-dir=/main/.git --work-tree=/main reset --hard` — the entry `git reset --hard @primary` is the exact thing this rule exists to refuse, but the tokens are `--git-dir=/main/.git` / `--work-tree=/main` (not `--git-dir` / `--work-tree`), so `_elsewhere` returns False, `is_primary(cwd)` returns False, and the command that resets the primary is allowed. The same class covers `GIT_DIR=/main/.git GIT_WORK_TREE=/main git reset --hard`, which contains no matching token at all. Since the new `-C` clause only makes sense if `matches()` skips leading option tokens (otherwise `git -C dir reset --hard` would never match the entry either), these attached-option commands do reach the `only_primary` branch and are wrongly let through.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_elsewhere (attached option forms)
